headline: P0158 (Family Practice, GA): 99215 share of 12.9% against 3.0% expected from patient complexity; elevated in almost every complexity stratum, including low-complexity patients with minor acute diagnoses
rationale: P0158 billed 60 of 465 claims (12.9%) as 99215. Given the panel's complexity, about 3.0% would be expected (risk-adjusted score 4.53). The z-score against peers is modest at 1.13. A sicker panel does not explain the excess. The provider's 99215 share is above the all-provider rate in 5 of 6 complexity strata: 0 conditions, 7.0% vs 2.1%; 1 condition, 7.7% vs 3.4%; 2 conditions, 21.1% vs 5.6%. Only the 3-condition stratum is lower (7.1% vs 8.7%). 21 of the 60 99215s (35%) went to patients with 0 or 1 chronic conditions. Many of the sampled low-complexity 99215s carry only a minor or acute diagnosis: rash R21 (C0072150, C0072175, C0072182), upper respiratory infection J06.9 (C0072226), follow-up exam Z09 (C0072204), and UTI N39.0 alone (C0071949, C0071988). The same depression patient was billed 99215 (C0072033) and, two days later, 99214 (C0072098). The high-complexity 99215s look more plausible (for example C0071997 and C0072064, each with 5 conditions), although even those strata run about 2.2-2.7x the peer rate. Overall coding also skews high: 99214 makes up 290 of 465 claims. This pattern is consistent with upcoding, but no clinical documentation, time records or MDM support were provided, and the claim lists are random samples only.
next_steps: Request medical records for the sampled low-complexity 99215s (e.g., C0072150, C0072175, C0072182, C0072226, C0072204, C0071949, C0071988) and audit MDM level or total time against 2021+ E/M guidelines.
Pull a statistically valid random sample of all 99215 claims, stratified by chronic-condition count, to estimate an error rate rather than relying on these samples.
Review the high-volume 99214 billing (62% of claims) for possible upcoding from 99213, especially on 0-1 condition patients.
Check whether 99215 visits are associated with prolonged services, time-based billing, or unlisted acute events that could justify the level.
Compare against the provider's prior-year E/M distribution and any payer education or prior audits.
